You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

I am doing a medical research paper and found this article. Summarize me introduction and epidemiology part in the bulleted points format. Keep it under 200 words.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

content:
1	Introduction
     2	 Staphylococcus aureus is a major bacterial human pathogen that causes a wide variety of clinical
     3	manifestations.[1] Infections are common both in community-acquired as well as hospital-acquired
     4	settings and treatment remains challenging to manage due to the emergence of multi-drug resistant
     5	strains such as MRSA (Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus).[2][3] S. aureus is found in the
     6	environment and is also found in normal human flora, located on the skin and mucous membranes (most
     7	often the nasal area) of most healthy individuals.[1] S. aureus does not normally cause infection on
     8	healthy skin; however, if it is allowed to enter the bloodstream or internal tissues, these bacteria
     9	may cause a variety of potentially serious infections.[1] Transmission is typically from direct
    10	contact. However, some infections involve other transmission methods.[4]
    11	
    12	
    13	 Go to:
    14	 Etiology
    15	 Staphylococcus aureus is Gram-positive bacteria (stain purple by Gram stain) that are cocci-shaped
    16	and tend to be arranged in clusters that are described as “grape-like.” On media, these organisms
    17	can grow in up to 10% salt, and colonies are often golden or yellow (aureus means golden or yellow).
    18	These organisms can grow aerobically or anaerobically (facultative) and at temperatures between 18 C
    19	and 40 C. Typical biochemical identification tests include catalase positive (all pathogenic
    20	Staphylococcus species), coagulase positive (to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from other
    21	Staphylococcus species), novobiocin sensitive (to distinguish from Staphylococcus saprophyticus),
    22	and mannitol fermentation positive (to distinguish from Staphylococcus epidermidis).[4][1] MRSA
    23	strains carry a mec gene on the bacterial chromosome, which is a component of the larger
    24	Staphylococcal chromosomal cassette mec (SCCmec) region, conferring resistance to multiple
    25	antibiotics depending on the SCCmec type.[2] The mec gene encodes the protein PBP-2a
    26	(penicillin-binding protein 2a). PBP-2a is a penicillin-binding protein (PBP), or essential
    27	bacterial cell wall enzyme that catalyzes the production of the peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell
    28	wall. PBP-2A has a lower affinity to bind to beta-lactams (and other penicillin-derived antibiotics)
    29	when compared to other PBPs, so PBP-2A continues to catalyze the synthesis of the bacterial cell
    30	wall even in the presence of many antibiotics. As a result, S. aureus strains that synthesize PBP-2A
    31	can grow in the presence of many antibiotics, and these MRSA strains are resistant to many
    32	antibiotics. MRSA strains tend to be resistant to methicillin, nafcillin, oxacillin, and
    33	cephalosporins.[2][4]
    34	
    35	
    36	 Go to:
    37	 Epidemiology
    38	 Staphylococcus aureus (including drug-resistant strains such as MRSA) are found on the skin and
    39	mucous membranes, and humans are the major reservoir for these organisms.[3][5] It is estimated that
    40	up to half of all adults are colonized, and approximately 15% of the population persistently carry
    41	S. aureus in the anterior nares. Some populations tend to have higher rates of S. aureus
    42	colonization (up to 80%), such as health care workers, persons who use needles on a regular basis
    43	(i.e., diabetics and intravenous (IV) drug users), hospitalized patients, and immunocompromised
    44	individuals. S. aureus can be transmitted person-to-person by direct contact or by fomites.[6][4][1]
    45	
    46	
    47	 Go to:
    48	 Pathophysiology
    49	 S. aureus are one the most common bacterial infections in humans and are the causative agents of
    50	multiple human infections, including bacteremia, infective endocarditis, skin and soft tissue
    51	infections (e.g., impetigo, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, cellulitis, scalded skin syndrome,
    52	and others), osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, prosthetic device infections, pulmonary infections
    53	(e.g., pneumonia and empyema), gastroenteritis, meningitis, toxic shock syndrome, and urinary tract
    54	infections.[6] Depending on the strains involved and the site of infection, these bacteria can cause
    55	invasive infections and/or toxin-mediated diseases.[6][7] The pathophysiology varies greatly
    56	depending on the type of S. aureus infection.[6] Mechanisms for evasion of the host immune response
    57	include the production of an antiphagocytic capsule, sequestering of host antibodies or antigen
    58	masking by Protein A, biofilm formation, intracellular survival, and blocking chemotaxis of
    59	leukocytes.[8][7] Binding of the bacteria to extracellular matrix proteins and fibronectin in
    60	infectious endocarditis is mediated by bacterial cell wall-associated proteins such as
    61	fibrinogen-binding proteins, clumping factors, and teichoic acids.[7] Also, Staphylococcal
    62	superantigens (TSST-1 or toxic shock syndrome toxin 1) are important virulence factors in infectious
    63	endocarditis, sepsis, as well as toxic shock syndrome.[9][10] Pneumonia infections are associated
    64	with the bacterial production of PVL (Panton-Valentine leukocidin), Protein A, and alpha-hemolysin,
    65	and infections are more common following influenza virus infection as well as a diagnosis of Cystic
    66	Fibrosis. Prosthetic device infections are often mediated by the ability of S. aureus strains to
    67	form biofilms as well as communicate using quorum sensing in a bacterial cell density-dependent
    68	manner. [11]

**Introduction**
- *Staphylococcus aureus* is "a major bacterial human pathogen" that causes a wide variety of clinical manifestations (doc.txt).
- Infections are common in both community-acquired and hospital-acquired settings, and treatment is challenging due to "the emergence of multi-drug resistant" strains such as MRSA (doc.txt).
- It is found in the environment and in normal human flora on the skin and mucous membranes, "most often the nasal area," of most healthy individuals (doc.txt).
- It does not normally infect healthy skin, but "if it is allowed to enter the bloodstream or internal tissues," it may cause potentially serious infections (doc.txt).
- "Transmission is typically from direct contact," though some infections involve other methods (doc.txt).

**Epidemiology**
- S. aureus, including drug-resistant strains such as MRSA, is found on the skin and mucous membranes, and "humans are the major reservoir for these organisms" (doc.txt).
- It is estimated that "up to half of all adults are colonized, and approximately 15% of the population persistently carry" S. aureus in the anterior nares (doc.txt).
- Higher colonization rates (up to 80%) occur in "health care workers, persons who use needles on a regular basis" (i.e., diabetics and IV drug users), hospitalized patients, and immunocompromised individuals (doc.txt).
- S. aureus "can be transmitted person-to-person by direct contact or by fomites" (doc.txt).
